notes.definition: When a simple (binary) ionic compound is electrolysed in the molten state using inert electrodes, the metal is produced at the cathode and the non-metal is produced at the anode. For example, molten lead bromide gives lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode.
explanation: A binary ionic compound contains just two elements: a metal and a non-metal, for example lead bromide (PbBr₂), sodium chloride (NaCl) or zinc chloride (ZnCl₂). When it is melted, the positive metal ions and negative non-metal ions are free to move, so the molten compound is an electrolyte. Because there is no water present, these are the only ions, which makes the products easy to predict.

The positive metal ions are attracted to the negative electrode (cathode). There they gain electrons and become metal atoms. The negative non-metal ions are attracted to the positive electrode (anode). There they lose electrons and form the non-metal element. Halide ions form diatomic molecules, such as Br₂ or Cl₂, and oxide ions form oxygen, O₂.

Lead bromide is a classic example because it melts at a fairly low temperature (about 370 °C), which can be reached with a Bunsen burner. Lead bromide is placed in a crucible with two graphite electrodes and heated until it melts; only then does the bulb or ammeter show a current flowing. Molten, shiny lead forms at the cathode and collects at the bottom of the crucible, and red-brown bromine vapour is given off at the anode. Overall: PbBr₂(l) → Pb(l) + Br₂(g).

Bromine vapour is toxic and corrosive, and lead and its compounds are toxic, so this experiment is done by a teacher in a fume cupboard, with eye protection, and the hot apparatus is left to cool. Graphite electrodes are used because they conduct electricity and are inert, so they do not react with the products.

To predict the products for any molten binary ionic compound, split the name into its two elements. The metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal forms at the anode. Molten potassium iodide gives potassium and iodine; molten zinc chloride gives zinc and chlorine; molten lithium oxide gives lithium and oxygen.
keyFacts: A binary ionic compound contains only two elements (a metal and a non-metal).
Molten ionic compounds conduct because their ions are free to move.
The metal is always produced at the cathode (negative electrode).
The non-metal is always produced at the anode (positive electrode).
Molten lead bromide gives lead at the cathode and bromine at the anode.
Bromine is seen as a red-brown vapour; lead as a shiny molten metal.
No current flows until the solid compound has melted.
The lead bromide electrolysis is done in a fume cupboard because bromine vapour is toxic.

keyTerms.definition: An ionic compound made of only two elements, such as lead bromide or sodium chloride.
Melted; in the liquid state because it has been heated above its melting point.
An electrode that conducts but does not react with the electrolyte or products, such as graphite.
The negative electrode, where metal ions gain electrons to form the metal.
The positive electrode, where non-metal ions lose electrons to form the non-metal.
A heat-resistant container used to hold a substance while it is heated to a high temperature.

workedExamples.question: Predict the products at each electrode when molten potassium iodide, KI, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes.
steps: Identify the ions: K⁺ (from the metal) and I⁻ (from the non-metal).
K⁺ is positive so it moves to the cathode and forms potassium.
I⁻ is negative so it moves to the anode and forms iodine, I₂.
workedExamples.answer: Potassium at the cathode; iodine at the anode.

workedExamples.title: Higher: writing the half equations
workedExamples.question: Write half equations for the reactions at each electrode during the electrolysis of molten zinc chloride, ZnCl₂.
steps: Cathode: each Zn²⁺ needs 2 electrons to become a Zn atom: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn.
Anode: two Cl⁻ ions each lose one electron to form one Cl₂ molecule: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻.
Check charges balance: left of cathode equation 2+ and 2−, total 0; anode: 2− on the left, 2− on the right.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the non-metal forms at the cathode because it is a gas.
misconceptions.right: In fact non-metal ions are negative, so they are attracted to the positive anode. The metal forms at the cathode.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think current flows through solid lead bromide.
misconceptions.right: In fact current only flows once the lead bromide has melted, because the ions must be free to move.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write bromine at the anode as Br.
misconceptions.right: In fact bromine is diatomic, so the product is Br₂. Chlorine is Cl₂, iodine is I₂ and oxygen is O₂.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think hydrogen can be produced from a molten compound.
misconceptions.right: In fact a molten binary compound contains no water, so only its own two elements are produced.

realWorld: Sodium metal is manufactured by electrolysing molten sodium chloride, which also produces chlorine.
Aluminium is extracted by electrolysing molten aluminium oxide, a binary ionic compound.
Reactive metals such as lithium and magnesium are produced by electrolysing their molten chlorides.
higherTier: Write half equations for the reactions at each electrode, for example cathode: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb; anode: 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻.
At the cathode the metal ions are reduced (gain electrons); at the anode the non-metal ions are oxidised (lose electrons).
examTips: To predict products, split the compound name: metal at the cathode, non-metal at the anode.
Remember diatomic elements: Cl₂, Br₂, I₂, O₂.
Describe observations precisely: 'red-brown vapour/gas at the anode', 'shiny silvery liquid metal at the cathode'.
Always explain why the compound must be molten: the ions must be free to move.
In half equations, check that the charges balance on both sides.
summary: Binary ionic compounds contain one metal and one non-metal.
They must be molten so the ions can move.
Metal forms at the cathode, non-metal at the anode.
Molten lead bromide gives lead (cathode) and bromine (anode).
Inert graphite electrodes are used; the experiment is done in a fume cupboard.

questions.explanation: Pb²⁺ ions are positive, so they move to the negative cathode and form lead. Bromine forms at the anode. There is no water, so no hydrogen or oxygen can form.

questions.question: Molten lead bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What is produced at the anode?
questions.explanation: Br⁻ ions are negative, so they move to the positive anode and form bromine. Lead forms at the cathode.

questions.question: Why must lead bromide be heated before it can be electrolysed?
options: To make it react with the electrodes
To melt it so the ions are free to move
To turn the ions into atoms
markScheme: 1 mark: to melt it so the ions are free to move
questions.explanation: Solid lead bromide has ions locked in a lattice. Melting frees the ions so they can move to the electrodes and carry the current.

questions.question: Molten potassium chloride is electrolysed. Which row shows the products?
questions.explanation: In a molten binary compound the metal forms at the cathode and the non-metal at the anode. Hydrogen and oxygen cannot form because there is no water.

questions.explanation: Bromine is released at the anode as red-brown vapour. The shiny liquid is lead at the cathode, and a gas that pops is hydrogen, which is not formed here.

questions.question: Why is the electrolysis of molten lead bromide carried out in a fume cupboard?
questions.explanation: Bromine vapour is toxic and corrosive, so it must be removed safely. Lead is not flammable and no hydrogen is produced.

questions.question: What is meant by a binary ionic compound?
options: An ionic compound containing two atoms
An ionic compound that conducts in two states
An ionic compound made of only two elements
An ionic compound with two positive ions
markScheme: 1 mark: made of only two elements
questions.explanation: Binary means two elements, such as lead and bromine in PbBr₂. PbBr₂ contains three ions, so binary does not mean two atoms or two ions.

questions.question: Which half equation shows the reaction at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead bromide?
questions.explanation: At the cathode the lead ions gain two electrons to become lead atoms. 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ is the anode reaction, Pb → Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ is the reverse reaction, and Pb²⁺ → Pb + 2e⁻ does not balance charge.

questions.question: Molten sodium iodide is electrolysed using inert electrodes. What forms at each electrode?
questions.explanation: Na⁺ ions go to the cathode and form sodium. I⁻ ions go to the anode and form iodine. Only the two elements in the compound can form because no water is present.

questions.question: Which half equation shows the reaction at the anode during the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: Two chloride ions each lose one electron to make one chlorine molecule. Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ is the reverse, Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na happens at the cathode, and Cl is not how chlorine exists (it is diatomic).

questions.question: At which electrode is a metal produced when a molten ionic compound is electrolysed?
questions.explanation: Metal ions are positive, so they are attracted to the negative cathode, where they form the metal.

questions.question: Name the metal formed when molten zinc bromide is electrolysed.
questions.explanation: Zinc bromide contains Zn²⁺ and Br⁻ ions. The metal, zinc, forms at the cathode.

questions.question: Molten copper chloride, CuCl₂, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. Name the product at the cathode and the product at the anode.
questions.explanation: Cu²⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and form copper. Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and form chlorine gas.

acceptedAnswers: molten ions free to move carry current
markScheme: 1 mark: in the solid the ions are fixed in place and cannot move
1 mark: when molten the ions are free to move and carry the current, so the circuit is complete
questions.explanation: The lamp lights only when charged particles can move through the electrolyte, which needs the lattice to be broken by melting.

questions.question:
Molten lead bromide is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Write a balanced symbol equation for the overall reaction.
Include state symbols.
questions.explanation: Lead bromide is molten, lead forms as a liquid at this temperature, and bromine is released as a gas (vapour): PbBr₂(l) → Pb(l) + Br₂(g).

questions.question:
Molten magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Write a half equation for the reaction at each electrode.
questions.explanation: Magnesium ions carry a 2+ charge, so need 2 electrons each. Two chloride ions lose one electron each to form one Cl₂ molecule.

questions.question: Predict the products at each electrode when molten lithium oxide, Li₂O, is electrolysed.
questions.explanation: Li⁺ ions go to the cathode and form lithium. O²⁻ ions go to the anode and form oxygen gas, O₂.

questions.question:
Molten lead bromide is electrolysed.
Bromine is produced at the anode.
Explain why the formation of bromine is described as oxidation.
markScheme: 1 mark: bromide ions lose electrons (2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻)
1 mark: oxidation is the loss of electrons
questions.explanation: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons. Each Br⁻ ion loses one electron to become a bromine atom, and two atoms join to form Br₂.

questions.question: Explain why graphite is used for the electrodes in the electrolysis of molten lead bromide.
acceptedAnswers: conducts electricity and does not react
markScheme: 1 mark: graphite conducts electricity and is inert (does not react with the electrolyte or products)
questions.explanation: An inert electrode means the only products are those from the electrolyte itself.

questions.question:
Molten lead bromide is electrolysed.
Give the colour of the bromine vapour produced at the anode.
questions.explanation: Bromine vapour is red-brown. This colour is a useful observation to identify the product at the anode.

markScheme: Indicative content: place solid lead bromide in a crucible (or heat-resistant container); insert two graphite (inert) electrodes connected to a d.c. power supply, with a lamp or ammeter in the circuit; heat strongly with a Bunsen burner until the lead bromide melts; lamp lights/current flows only when molten because ions are free to move; Pb²⁺ ions attracted to the cathode, Br⁻ ions to the anode; at the cathode shiny/silvery molten lead forms and collects at the bottom; at the anode red-brown bromine vapour is given off; carry out in a fume cupboard because bromine is toxic; wear eye protection; let apparatus cool before handling; lead compounds are toxic.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): clear, logically sequenced method including melting, correct observations at both electrodes linked to the movement of ions, and relevant safety precautions with reasons.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method including heating to melt, with at least one correct observation and one safety precaution.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as lead forms or bromine forms, or heat the lead bromide.
questions.explanation: A complete answer links method, observations and explanation: the compound only conducts when molten, positive lead ions form lead at the cathode, negative bromide ions form bromine at the anode, and the toxic bromine requires a fume cupboard.

questions.question:
Molten sodium bromide, NaBr, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes.
Explain how the products form at each electrode.
Your answer should include half equations and identify which species is oxidised and which is reduced.
markScheme: 1 mark: Na⁺ ions are attracted to the cathode and Br⁻ ions to the anode
1 mark: cathode: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (sodium forms)
1 mark: sodium ions are reduced (gain electrons) and bromide ions are oxidised (lose electrons)
questions.explanation: Sodium ions gain one electron each (reduction) and bromide ions lose one electron each (oxidation). Two bromine atoms combine to form Br₂, so two bromide ions appear in the anode half equation.

questions.question:
A molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Table 1 shows the products.
Which compound was electrolysed?
questions.explanation: The products of a molten binary compound are its two elements, so the compound is calcium bromide (CaBr₂). Calcium bromate contains oxygen and is not binary.

questions.question:
A molten compound X is electrolysed using inert electrodes.
Table 1 shows the observations.
Suggest what type of compound X is.
Explain your answer.
markScheme: 1 mark: the pale green gas is chlorine, which comes from chloride ions at the anode
1 mark: so X is a metal chloride (for example sodium chloride or lead chloride), with the metal forming at the cathode
questions.explanation: Chlorine is a pale green gas, so X contains chloride ions. The silvery metal at the cathode shows X contains metal ions, so X is a molten metal chloride.
